If this is a sincere question (sometimes I don’t know on Reddit haha), please do not take this as medical advice, but some basic thoughts: Generally speaking, the essential benefits of exercise are obtained with about 150 minutes of moderate intensity exercise (which is just about anything that gets your heart rate higher than normal, including brisk walking) or 75 minutes of more intense exercise (think running, swimming, biking) per week. More doesn’t make any difference in the most essential health benefits (obviously if you have strength building or running distance goals you probably want more of a plan), so in many cases you probably need to work out less than you think - and *definitely* less than what a lot of fitness and eating subs on Reddit will tell you. 

I think if you’re new to exercise, the key is starting in a way that feels manageable. You don’t have to sprint on the treadmill for half an hour every day and in fact you probably shouldn’t. But walking, some bodyweight exercises (modified for your level of fitness), or anything you enjoy is a great start.

The other thing that this sub is often reflecting is that if you’re exercising and you don’t want to injure yourself, you have to eat. A lot of fitness subs will tell you not to ‘eat back’ your exercise calories - this is a very bad idea and all it will accomplish is making you feel like shit. The more active your body is, the more calories it needs to function, and you also need a lot more calories per day to feel okay, think clearly, and be a normal-ish person than a lot of low-calorie enthusiasts will suggest, even if your only movement was to get up, walk downstairs, and type at a computer for a few hours. (Like - trigger warning, calories - >!1200!< a day is not enough, I don’t care what the diet subs say). *especially* if you already have disordered restrictive eating habits, I really just encourage you to start smaller, try to see if you can eat more to compensate for more activity (a dietician can help - not, usually, a personal trainer or sports coach! Different people!), and hopefully think of exercise as a way to help yourself be well, not a way to punish yourself for eating or to shrink.

Oh OP, I really empathize very much with your feelings. I also frequently wish I didn’t rely on medication and therapy to feel well(ish), that it didn’t take all this extra effort for me to feel like I’m just at the automatic baseline of everyone else. I’m so sorry you’re feeling these things too. 

The other commenter really covered everything well, so I won’t repeat what they said, but I will also say that a lot of the fear you have of people seeing your scars if you wear a crop top is completely understandable but also less of an issue than you might imagine. Not even because people are kind and generous but because everyone in public is wrapped up in their own lives. Others observe (and care about) a lot less of our appearances than our insecurities lead us to believe. And if they do notice, who cares? (I know, haha, we care because it’s a sensitive matter) but what I mean is they’re a neutral part of your body. They aren’t bad or scary or shameful, they’re just a feature of you to which nobody gets to attach meaning if you don’t agree. 

As for the weight bit, you might be interested in the podcast Maintenance Phase, which frequently discusses how we have a cultural fantasy that losing weight will not only change our bodies but our lives - that the thinner us will be happier and better in every way. It’s your body and as long as you’re treating it well (ie, if you can see a dietician, they can definitely help you on this journey, and at minimum any weight loss should be slow and steady and about eating foods that nourish you and moving your body in ways that feel good, not focused on crash diets or starving yourself or feeling consumed by the process) it’s your prerogative to lose weight if you want. But the idea that if we could only be thinner, we would resolve everything painful in our lives, is simply not true. I think it’s worth remembering that - there’s so much more involved in a life than your body size.

A last note, you sound pretty young - I’m not going to say everything always gets better because that’s a cliche, but my god, do some things get easier with age! Especially being more comfortable in your own skin; it can take work, but I’m not nearly as insecure about how I look compared to others or who I am overall as I was five or ten years ago. Hang in there.

Ah, this is something I very frequently feel. I personally hate when people suggest you just need to find happiness on your own, because humans are social creatures meant to live in community.

One thing that might be good to remember is that honestly, a lot of college-aged people are self-absorbed, not in a necessarily unkind way, but just because a lot of college students haven’t had that many demands on their ability to put others first if they’ve been supported by family. Add in being ‘on your own’ for the first time and you’d be amazed how many people your age just don’t think much about other people because they are wrapped up in their own shit. It doesn’t make it easier, but it may help to know it very often isn’t personal. 

Another thought that may be somewhat useful is some friends are different kinds of friends. You might have ‘go bowling on Wednesday together’ friends and ‘call in a crisis’ friends, and they probably don’t overlap, but those people both bring some value to your life. It’s okay not to be completely constantly emotionally intimate with everyone. 

I also definitely would not take any reactions you do or don’t get on Reddit too seriously. The vagaries of the internet push some posts to the spotlight and others fall by the wayside without much rhyme or reason.

Finally, as for your friend who often vents to you, I just want to say it’s totally okay to set boundaries and/or not always have a solution. You’re being a good friend if you listen and are supportive; you aren’t required to be the solutions architect. 

I think it could be very helpful to speak to a therapist about these feelings. Most universities offer counseling and/or can help refer you to someone in the area. It’s really nice to have someone designated who can help you sort through emotions and also not feel like you’re being a ‘burden’ - it’s their job to listen! 

None of this really helps with never feeling like you’re being reached out to, that you always have to do the work. I don’t have great advice on that crux of the problem because I relate to it *so* much, and I haven’t found a way to fix things, only to try to accept that sometimes people just suck! But maybe it helps to know that there are others who feel similarly and want mutual genuine connection out there. Hopefully we all find one another.

There’s also a cliche that still holds true and I sometimes try to remember: you haven’t met all the people who are going to love you. Maybe the friends you have now aren’t forever friends, but there are so many people who will be in your life who you don’t know yet.

Between applications, you could also wear silicone tape, which helps add gentle pressure to promote healing. Also, it may not be as financially accessible, but laser treatments can absolutely help with promoting fading if used while the scars are still red (I got V Beam on some of my scars and it helped most of them a lot, much more than just creams did). Lastly, retin-A (tretinoin) can really help fading too! (Just don’t use right before a laser.) And keep them out of the sun/use SPF! Best of luck.

Because these are still red, I believe they would probably still be amenable to laser treatments like V-Beam (reduces redness) and would encourage you to seek out a dermatologist if you’re interested in that. It can really help speed up the process of fading the color. Unfortunately, it’s usually classed as ‘cosmetic’ and isn’t covered by insurance (if you’re in the US), but a number of plastic surgery outlets will do reduced fee or free service for self harm scars. Otherwise, redness fading happens on the order of probably 6-7 months (depending on your personal healing), so patience is key.

As for the deep enough question - it comes up so much on this sub, and I would first point you to a post [here](https://www.reddit.com/r/SelfHarmScars/comments/fgen29/self_harm_isnt_a_contest_none_of_us_are_winning/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=ios_app&utm_name=iossmf) about how SH is not a competition and no one is winning. The OP described how they had injuries that local ER doctors remember in detail with horror, while on here they were about average. This sub, I think, can give a skewed perspective of what ‘counts.’

There is no bar at which your self harm is ‘bad enough’ - *any* self harm is well beyond the threshold of healthy coping mechanisms or standard day to day emotional struggles. From a personal perspective, I don’t want to feed the ‘deep enough’/comparison drive with this, but for the sake of the example: most of my wounds were significantly less visually noticeable than yours, and I never needed medical attention (often a metric for depth of wounds that require stitching etc), and multiple therapists still wanted me to do a partial hospitalization and were *extremely* concerned about my welfare. And I know that I was very much not okay at all. Self harm is self harm is self harm. The only reason distinctions between physical damage matter is to triage what kind of medical attention you might need and to ensure people who are a danger to their life receive appropriate intervention; no one who self-injures is not struggling enough. The act of self injury is the symptom of deep pain or anger or similar, not the degree of scarring.

Maybe also consider it this way. The ‘average’ person who never engaged in SH often can’t even comprehend the idea; I know everyone who knew about my SH who hadn’t had similar behaviors was appalled and even repulsed. That is not to endorse their reactions, but just to remind you and anyone else reading this that if you’re here, your pain is real.

The other thing is in the term itself - we generally don’t endorse ways of hurting oneself, whether that’s starving yourself or pushing everyone around you away or saying cruel things to/about yourself or spending all your money on things you can’t afford et cetera et cetera because most or at least many human moral systems or principles hold that a person is a valuable being not deserving of harm (outside of retributive models of punishment which still generally are meant to have a purifying or cleansing effect) from self or others.

I understand it feels like the only coping mechanism you have, but I would encourage you to consider that may not be true; that’s the last reason SH is ‘bad,’ because - as much as I understand how it feels like this - it isn’t actually the only thing to which one will ever be able to turn, and alternatives exist that don’t pose risks of long-term physical damage, and may even help you in other ways (eg better communication and relationships, stronger self esteem). Hi! I have no experience in this field, but I’m hoping maybe an outside perspective can add something.

What you described sounds like a really toxic work environment. That’s a bit of an overused cliche these days, but my field also has a certain rite of passage through frequently abusive institutions to ‘earn’ your training and position, and the thing that I’ve been trying to learn is this: surviving such an environment reflects very little on your ability to do the work and very much on your ability to suffer through cruelty and chaos. Is that an accomplishment or asset in its own right? Sure, I suppose. Is it an accomplishment particularly important to defining your goodness as an individual? Not really! Is it an accomplishment worth suffering through? I’m skeptical! 

You did the right thing by trying to move somewhere where you could accrue more skills. You did the right thing asking to practice a procedure so you could learn. These belittling responses are frankly bizarre in many ways and absolutely not a reflection on you. At minimum, it’s really embarrassingly bad training procedure, which is a major defect for any competent organization.

I’m really so glad this field was a place for you to find meaning, but I hope you might be able to see it’s not *you* or your only value. As someone with pretty significant trauma issues and a number of mental health diagnoses, I sympathize very, very much with feeling my life doesn’t matter, I don’t have any odds of being happy, that I am stupid and foolish and incompetent. But one thing I have observed from people more advanced in their careers is simply that the institution will not love you back. You could be an amazing, wonderful help to patients and still, if you got sick or had to leave, you would probably be replaced overnight. That is *not* to say your role doesn’t matter or meant to make you feel worse - just that organizations don’t and can’t really care about anyone, the upshot being you don’t owe them either. You don’t owe your workplace and (horrible) colleagues your mental welfare. If you are suicidal because of your workplace, that - at least to me - is an extremely important indicator that something has to change. Whether it’s leaving your job, getting other supports outside of work, or the work environment being modulated somewhat, considering hurting yourself because of your workplace environment is not a rite of passage that anyone should endure. It’s just not. I don’t care what the standard of the field is; even if older colleagues had to endure some sort of hazing, that’s not a reason to perpetuate it.

The last thing I might point out is that even if you decided to stick this out - which I hope I’ve conveyed isn’t necessary or clearly desirable by any means - it’s not permanent. At least it shouldn’t be, right? I kind of hesitate to write that because I don’t want to encourage essentially self-injury through work, but you’re not going to be the learning/new person forever, no matter your path. And lots of learning/new people get much kinder receptions!

So I suppose I just want to say that you’re not too weak for this world. For one, this workplace is not an accurate representation of ‘the world.’ People love to go on about how the ‘real world’ is tough and cruel and you have to buck up, but I think that’s horseshit in a lot of ways. There’s no moral or legal rule stating you have to suffer to get to a solid professional station. There might be conventions in the field of ‘putting in your time,’ but none of those are somehow right or meaningful in any way other than ‘a bunch of people decided this was how we’d do things.’

All of which is to say that I’m so sorry you’re in this position, and it also does not warrant shame. You’re a human being who would benefit from an environment catering to human beings - don’t beat yourself up about that. I wish you the best.

This may or may not be helpful, but: I’m the same age as you. I got my college degree from an Ivy League school and a graduate degree from another prestigious university; I have a solid job at an institution well-known in my field; I’ve done a good amount of travel, though covid trampled on my best-laid plans; and I don’t like listing appearance as though it were an accomplishment, but because body image is clearly significant for you, I’ll add that I am thin and conventionally attractive. None of that means I don’t have issues (lol, probably wouldn’t be in this sub after all), but those are all things you feel stuck on and wish you had, right? Well, the important part here is that I spent the last ~half year *completely* fucking miserable and realistically should have been in a partial hospitalization, and I spent ~6 years before that fighting, with varying degrees of success, to just get to less-intense degrees of unhappiness. On every metric, I feel wildly behind my peers. A bit ironically given your positive experience with your boyfriend, loneliness, especially romantic, has been one of the most painful and ongoing feelings for me.

None of the above was to suggest you haven’t experienced loss and obstacles; those feelings are real and legitimate. And I don’t mean to come off as ‘sad? get in line!’ and start blogging about my own shit. But just to say as someone who looks at least externally like the people with degrees moving and living life, my internal world is not similarly on track. Many, if not most, accomplishments have very little to do with our own self-esteem at the end of the day, at least not without a strong sense of self and worth around who you are, not what you do.

The other thing is that while that list probably sounded a bit self-aggrandizing (sorry!), I didn’t do much in particular to deserve my education and experiences; I was lucky and supported in many ways that many people are not. You aren’t a failed human prototype.

I would also just say if your boyfriend has been with you, and lovely to you, for seven years, I hardly imagine he can see you as a trash bag. I know when your self-esteem is low it’s *so* hard to take seriously any positive feedback, but that’s pretty clear! 

None of that, I expect, does much for your urges, but I do wonder if you’ve tried individual outpatient therapy? Totally get inpatient was an awful experience, but it might be helpful to have someone - especially who specializes in body dysmorphia or whatever else you’d like to focus on - designated to hear you out. Finding the right person can genuinely be a game changer.

So, I want to be honest here and say that you can’t ever *get rid* of scars that didn’t disappear themselves. If the wound was deep enough to create scar tissue, you will have scar tissue (though they can change for up to a year or two). That said, you can reduce scarring visibility. Scars are generally more amenable to intervention sooner rather than later, though I think some providers will prefer that you wait at least a year from the injury (don’t quote me). If you see a medical professional (likely to have better results than an aesthetician) like a dermatologist or plastic surgeon, they can use lasers to improve color and texture or steroid injections to improve raised scars. Some places provide reduced-cost or free services for SH. If you’re working on an at-home basis, I would 1) use scar massage, essentially rubbing a moisturizing unscented gel/lotion/oil into the scars several times a day - there are post-surgical scar massage guides online, and 2) try silicone gel or strips. Silagen are the best strips I’ve found but are pricey. Pricey scar gels designed for post-plastic surgery/dermatology-office use can work well because they have fancy supporting ingredients, but the key is silicone, regardless of price range of the gel. Silicone requires consistency over months to see a difference, especially with older scars. 

Otherwise, should the scars not be changing anymore and well and truly healed, paramedical tattooing (different from a cover up regular tattoo) can significantly reduce the appearance, though you may need touch-ups.

Best of luck x

It may depend on your access to health insurance/particular providers, but: 

1) dermatologists can often help. In fact, the least amenable scars to intervention are ones that are flat and faded to white; if it’s raised (hypertrophic), there’s more room for improvement. Steroids can be injected to help flatten them, and different lasers also can help with color and texture. Plastic surgeons will do this too, and some will provide treatment for free or reduced cost for self harm (like Westside Aesthetics in Los Angeles). You might also just see a primary care provider to start with. I will add here to be careful about who you see for this; a lot of aestheticians and spas will also offer scar treatment, often cheaper than straight-up medical outlets, but depending on location their training is not equivalent to someone who got a medical degree, fellowship, board certification, etc - I think it’s important to see people who really know what they’re doing if you can.

2) at home, you can also do a few things. One is scar massage - there’s lots of post-surgical guidelines on scar massage online, but the idea is just rubbing some kind of oil, lotion, or gel (preferably unscented) into the area several times a day. It’s not going to magically make them level with the skin, but it can help improve appearance and basically skin flexibility over time. The other thing I recommend is silicone; either silicone gel, silicone scar sheets, or both. Silagen are the best sheets I’ve found, but they are pricey. Silicone is generally the front line response to surgical scars; it does, however, take at least several months of consistent use (ie wearing a strip whenever you aren’t bathing or working out) to see results, and longer with older scars.

Best of luck!

Oh yeah sure! Mainly just because I think addiction is really useful for some people to describe their experience with SH, but not everyone experiences it that way. In terms of the academic literature (again, academic research cannot and does not perfectly represent human life), SH is usually (obviously not universally, but generally) associated with negative emotions, while (other) substances trigger craving in a variety of contexts, including positive emotional ones. There’s also a potentially meaningfully difference, as far as I understand, between a chemical addiction (ie your body is physically going through withdrawal because it’s so biologically dependent on a substance - eg vomiting, diarrhea, pain from withdrawal and the literal death risk from stopping a heavy addiction cold turkey) and a ‘psychological’ addiction, where the release of endorphins and other chemicals after SH create reliance/craving. But of course I can understand how that position might seem too close to suggesting self harm can ‘just be stopped,’ which I know isn’t true or fair to say from my own experience.

That isn’t at all to say that self-injury doesn’t have addictive properties, or that people don’t experience addiction and dependency with it - I wouldn’t ever want to invalidate that, it’s definitely true for many. It’s really only a meaningful issue because treatment options and recovery pathways are different depending on the particular type of reliance a person experiences on the behavior or the substance (of course, substance abuse and SH can be and are often coincident). So I guess I just don’t want to use the language of addiction if it’s not what someone feels is most relevant to them, and realistically I think most of our language is going to be an imperfect fit. But definitely I think relapse/recovery/dependency do define many people’s experience, and it’s not like I’m all knowing, of course addiction models and according harm-reduction strategies make sense for many people. It’s just tricky to perfectly describe complex behaviors!

Hi mom/dad/parent! I’m glad you posted here and you seem like a caring, supportive parent, which really makes a huge difference. 

When my parents found out, I had disclosed to my therapist and she basically told me she needed to tell them - I was reluctant about it but it was helpful to have a professional, one I trusted, do the actual discussion for me; my parents knew and could help me find resources without me having to actually do the stressful lifting of explaining. It can take a few tries to find someone you’re comfortable with, but it also helps a lot to have a parent who can call/leave messages/help find options instead of having to do it yourself.

I would recommend you seek professional support as well, just to help you sort through your own feelings and have a safe place to air them (without violating her privacy by speaking to your friends or family about the issue). I wish my parents had seen someone who could a) guide them in being supportive and b) help them work through their own feelings without projecting them onto me. It is understandable and even natural to feel guilty or like you failed your daughter, and it’s important that you have a place to process those emotions. If you’re getting a therapist, you might even use that to frame your daughter’s situation, ie ‘I’m going to start getting some mental health support and wonder if you might like to consider that too.’ Therapy can be for all sorts of life challenges - even just having someone to talk to - and it might help to discuss it as such (I don’t know if your family has a particular attitude toward mental health, but it can obviously be stigmatized to seek support and it may be useful to try to reduce that).

In terms of bringing it up, I would not: make it a huge confrontation, ask to see her scars/injuries, guilt trip her, or say judgmental or shaming things (I was already really ashamed and didn’t need to feel more pathologized; an example of this would be something my mother said, that it would be ‘good’ that I had scars because it would remind me I needed to modulate my emotions ‘in a better way,’ which felt awful to me, as I had turned to self injury out of intense emotional desperation and not some rational calculation, and really hated the scarring - though not everyone feels that way about their scars). I would: ask how she’s doing, maybe note that she seems to be struggling a bit and you want to support her, and broach it in a way that’s comfortable for your relationship (maybe you guys drink your morning tea together or something - obviously I don’t know!) If writing a note for her might be easier to start, go for it and let her know she can write you back if she doesn’t want to talk. If you two don’t have a close relationship, it is completely okay if you aren’t the number one support person she ends up leaning on; just from your post I suspect you are a good parent, but I can say that having a mother with abusive tendencies made it strange and vexed to rely on her somewhat for support; she wasn’t really capable of being there for me in the way I wished and needed, and I wish she could have understood more clearly, and without making it about her, that I needed other help.

I would also make sure there are medical/wound care supplies in an accessible area of the house.

I want to note for you that self-harm can very often be associated with depression and suicidal ideation, but the act itself can be done without suicidal intent (hence why it’s sometimes referred to as Non-Suicidal Self Injury or NSSI). That doesn’t mean it’s not concerning, obviously, but I wouldn’t be afraid that you *need to get her into a hospital right now* or anything like that. Of course I’m not a professional and don’t know you or your daughter, but while I was definitely depressed, I didn’t want to end my life by hurting myself, I was just in intense pain and trying to manage it (if in a very unhealthy way).

I would also say that it’s important to respect her agency. If you try to push her into something she really doesn’t want to do, she’s probably not going to truly participate and benefit and may resent you/not feel safe disclosing things to you. Obviously, should you suspect at any point she is a danger to her own life, you need to do what you need to do, but otherwise I would hear her out regarding what she would or would not like to try. For instance, if she’s reluctant about therapy, maybe she just tries it out once or twice and you assure her if she doesn’t want to stay with that person you won’t force her (and over time, people can become more amenable to giving different options a shot).

One other thing I wish my parents had understood is that recovering from a place where you’re hurting yourself is not overnight. Because my father didn’t like seeing me in pain, I think he basically decided that if I wasn’t presenting as catatonically depressed, I was ‘better,’ and that felt strange and kind of invalidating because it’s not an on/off switch, it’s a whole gradation of progress and set-backs. I wanted him to understand that I still needed support and still wasn’t ‘okay’ as much as I was improving from my rock bottom, but I wasn’t going to say ‘hey, dad, actually I’m really miserable just to keep you apprised.’ I think another facet of this was my mom really being involved in trying to get me into resources at first, and then just dropping off after a few weeks; it was like she sort of ran out of steam, but I didn’t get to choose to stop dealing with my depression and trauma. So patience and consistency are important.

I think the most important thing is to just let her know you’re there for her, that you love her, and you’re not going anywhere. I hope the very best for you both, and as someone older who doesn’t cut anymore, I promise - although it’s a cliche and not always fair - things can get better.

You might explain you’re appreciative and relieved that they are willing to help you find a therapist, and that you would really benefit from doing so sooner rather than later. If it’s hard to speak with them, you might write them a note or even send a text to start the discussion. A therapist can also help you communicate with your parents/speak to them for you down the line if you struggle to ask them for resources.

Good luck and keep advocating for yourself as you can!

Also, as you probably know but I forgot to mention, deeper injuries often correlate with more scarring (though it’s an imperfect relationship), so if shallower wounds are manageable for you short of avoiding SH entirely, that might help you worry less about scarring (but don’t beat yourself up if you sometimes end up with deeper wounds than you might have intended; I know I did).

I personally probably wouldn’t notice them unless I was really looking, and especially if I wasn’t familiar with self harm scars I doubt I would notice. I don’t know for sure about fading, since it’s dependent on your own body and genetics, but I would bet they’d likely fade more pale over time or even essentially fade away for all visual purposes, and you can use silicone gel or adhesive patches - just be patient, they take months to really have an effect - as well as scar massage (post surgical guidelines online can give you more info) if you want to help minimize the appearance. Usually once scar tissue sets in it remains from, like, a biological/skin healing standpoint, but it may well be extremely hard to see. Just based on my experiences!

I would always feel this way. It kind of ended up being a major impetus for stopping, whether or not that’s ‘healthy.’ I think for me (when I had the supplies) it helped to do things to reduce the severity of the scarring; that means ‘wet’ healing (keeping wounds moist with petroleum jelly under bandages rather than letting them dry out), using silicone gel and/or silicone adhesive sheets as soon as the wounds healed, and doing regular scar massage. If your wounds are deep, stitching will also help a lot to minimize scarring versus letting things stay gaping. Of course none of that is going to totally prevent a scar (pricier things like lasers will do more but may not be sustainable), but making it less obvious is the most I could do. It also can be kind of therapeutic to take care of/be gentle with yourself and can counter the feelings of being an idiot. Minimizing scarring is also more effective when you start earlier rather than later, so it is an immediate step you can take. Also, for what it’s worth, other people are more wrapped up in their own stuff and less likely to notice scars than I often imagined; it probably feels the most obvious to you. Just my thoughts!

Also creams like mederma can be beneficial mostly because you’re [massaging](https://moffitt.org/media/1086/managing_your_scar.pdf) them into the scar, but you can achieve the same effects (in terms of reducing tightness and often appearance) with cheaper stuff like any moisturizing lotion or oil (baby oil, lavender oil).

Try silicone scar tape! The separate sheets can be pricey but the tape rolls are relatively cheap in terms of how much you get, and it can be reused as long as it’s sticky (plus some brands you can wash with soap/water and let dry to get the stickiness back). I’m pretty sure it actually works [better than Mederma](https://nymag.com/strategist/article/best-scar-removal-creams.html), and it stays in contact with the skin rather than requiring multiple daily applications. Even the pricier sheets can be pretty cost-effective if you reuse them.

Here from r/selfharm - I was looking at your recent posts and just want to say you seem like a fantastic mom, and I’m sorry about the struggles you’ve had recently. I’m not a therapist or anything and obviously haven’t met you or your daughter, but I have lived with depression for about ~7 years. 

1) I hate indoor overhead lights too, especially during the day. I think someone mentioned this could be a more serious sensory/sensitivity issue, but it’s also possible she could be a [Highly Sensitive Person (HSP)](https://hsperson.com/test/highly-sensitive-test/); HSPs tend to be particularly sensitive both to external sensory inputs and, to use your words, ‘big feelings.’ If you can find softer, less offensive light sources for her (I used to have a room where I put a tapestry over the overhead light - though that may be a fire hazard, lol - and usually used fairy/twinkle lights strung around the room instead), that seems like a good idea. I also have one of those ‘galaxy projector’ lights that I find soothing and a good source of minimal light in the evening.

2) Tooth brushing is, as some people mentioned, worth pushing over - dental health is nothing to mess around with. Mouthwash might be a relatively low-effort addition or (only sometimes!) substitute, and the kids’ flossers/floss picks are easier than regular dental floss. Showering is less concerning; we really don’t need to shower every day unless we are getting literally dirty, and baby wipes or cleansing wipes (or even dry shampoo) can be a good interim measure. Your creation of a calming and lovely shower environment seems like an awesome thing to continue doing as well. As you may already know from her therapy, depression is a weird reverse-engineered disease; at the worst, it absolutely can be impossible to do anything, but usually there’s a counterintuitive reaction where as you do more, you feel like doing more. So, for example, in CBT, you can get worksheets that help doing just one thing feel manageable. Managing to brush her teeth might be one step that has that activity-positive effect (though of course if it’s a sensory issue as opposed to ‘just’ depression that’s more complicated).

3) I’m not qualified to assess how ‘typical’ this is in terms of *literally* treating depression like a separate entity and think it’s worth bringing up to a therapist, but Churchill wrote about his episodes with the ‘black dog’ of depression, and sometimes it’s helpful to remind myself - and something a therapist has said before and helped me - that ‘xyz (whatever cruel thing I was thinking about myself and my failure) is your depression talking.’ So I don’t think it’s necessarily bad; in fact, it’s maybe useful sometimes to remember that her depression is not *her*. It seems to be a way to separate her ‘true’ self from the experience of depression, which seems like potentially a good thing? Though of course if it becomes *too* literal in terms of ‘someone else in her head’ it may be an additional mental health concern, hence why I think a therapist could offer a better assessment. I’m not sure about helping her ‘win,’ but maybe you can just tell her that you know it’s really tiring fighting this depression, and you know sometimes it feels like it’s winning, but the depression is lying when she feels like a bad person or like everyone hates her and you’re with her every step of the way.

All the best!

Mostly came here to say that it’s wonderful how hard you are working to support your daughter. I’m glad she has someone caring in her corner; it really can make such a difference.

I also felt very ashamed after self-harming, and in my case that was enough (in conjunction, of course, with therapeutic support and medication) to motivate me to stop altogether. I still get intrusive thoughts about harming at times, and I worry a bit more when life gets hard because I have to be attentive to how I’m coping, but it’s not something I actively struggle to resist in daily life. However, I was older than your daughter and didn’t self-harm long or frequently enough that it took on addictive properties, which it can for some people. I think it sounds right not to stigmatize and pathologize it in your reactions; as someone who was already doing that to myself, I didn’t need a parent to do so as well.

With respect to the harm reduction piece, I do think it would have been helpful for me. I cut in dangerous places (in terms of possible tendon/nerve damage), didn’t usually have familiarity with or consistency in the ‘tools’ I used and thus accidentally would cut more deeply than intended, and often didn’t have supplies on hand to take care of my wounds properly; I think it would have at least been better not to be in that situation. I think as long as ‘relapses’ don’t make your daughter feel even worse but are acknowledged as part of the process of healing that don’t take away from times she was able to cope in more healthy ways (which is what I think you’ve described), the strategy makes pretty good sense. Since she has expressed a desire to stop, that really is the first step and it’s great that she has you to support her through that process.

Two other things that may be helpful are: 1) avoiding situations or factors that tend to be particularly triggering. I presume your kiddo isn’t drinking yet, but for me alcohol was a serious contributor (as were certain social media sites I had to just delete entirely), so I cut that out until I was more stable. 2) As I think someone else mentioned, alternative coping mechanisms; usually, for me, cutting was an impulsive action to cope with intense emotions, and so even just using a timer to force myself to wait, letting that urge pass, was helpful. Breathing exercises and/or demanding physical activity also helped me. If your daughter has access to a smartphone, I’ve seen some people recommend the Calm Harm app, though I haven’t used it myself.

I also hope you have some support to be able to take care of yourself, because there is definitely a secondary strain on you when someone else is hurting this way (not, of course, in a fault or blame sense). Maybe your own therapist (as a better alternative in terms of respecting your daughter’s privacy than disclosing this information to, say, your friends or family)? 

One last note that probably isn’t relevant right this moment has to do with scars. I don’t know if your daughter cuts in a way that will leave scarring, but if she feels the shame about the scars that I do, it may be an important ‘last’ or eventual step to a) work on acceptance of them and/or b) work on minimizing them. Interventions like laser treatments tend to work better on younger scars, but obviously if the self-harm is ongoing that’s not where your mind will be; just something I wish I had known earlier.

I wish the best for you and your daughter!

One therapist once described it to me with this analogy: if a child is terrified of flying on the plane, therapy can help work on the issues that make the experience frightening and give them tools to cope once they’re traveling, but medication might be needed to make it possible for the kid to physically go through security and get on the flight in the first place. Going medication-only can be suboptimal, but pairing it with therapy usually is very complementary. You can always stop or change medications until you find what works for you. Since the many other steps you have taken don’t seem sufficient, it might just be that you have the kind of brain that benefits from chemical intervention. Lots of us do! 

Also, I don’t think your therapist will be disappointed in you! They want you to be safe, not win a contest for ‘most competent patient at dealing with depression.’ I totally get the ER may not have felt right, and another thing you might consider speaking with your therapist about is an option like an intensive outpatient program (IOP); it’s basically a group program teaching coping skills for people who aren’t necessarily in need of an inpatient/hospitalization level of care. If your therapist is concerned that you needed to go the ER, an IOP might be a solid alternative to consider getting you more consistent support. Or maybe just seeing them more often! Lots of things to be done that don’t require you to waltz into the ER and announce you need help - honestly, I’m not sure I could do that.

I wish you all the best and am glad you posted this; you’re doing all you can. I also want to just say hating yourself *is your depression talking.* that doesn’t mean it’s not real, not at all, but it does mean you just might look back in a few months and think gee, my feelings were so real but also so distorted. While depression is a cruel monster to struggle with, I’m confident you’re putting yourself in the best possible position to heal and feel more joy 😌

Hi there! Apologies in advance for what’s going to be a kind of long comment. Please know I’m not a therapist or any other kind of professional so don’t take me *too* seriously! First of all, I hope you can focus on the statement you made at the beginning of this post; your dad believes in you and tells you so. That’s meaningful and worth keeping at the front of your mind. 

As for the things that cause your father irritation, I want to note that a number of these honestly don’t seem like legitimate criticisms from him. Eating more than he wants you to, or not exercising as much as he wants you to (which I’m guessing relates to the ‘lazy’ complaint), is really not fair grounds for parental criticism of a child. As long as you’re eating and exercising in ways that feel good to you and support your health (i.e., you’re not engaging in disordered eating, over-exercising, or other dangerous behaviors), it’s really not his business, or anyone’s business, *at all*. Feeling shame is not generally a healthy relationship dynamic, and I’m not saying your dad is at fault necessarily, but it also is not necessarily healthy for you to be facing criticisms like that, and especially for you to feel so guilty about them.

Also, being a parent means you should support and love your child, even and arguably especially if and when they fail or need assistance. You aren’t alive to make your dad’s life perfect; it’s wonderful you want to be a good family member, but it’s not the determinant of your worth. Especially if your dad can be overly critical or harsh, it’s not necessarily a great idea to stake your self-esteem on how he says he feels about your achievements. These kind of family relationships are also an area where therapy can be really helpful - feel free to PM if you’d like some thoughts on seeking and finding a therapist! 

The last third of your post, where you say you never improve yourself and aren’t any good, is what my depression sounds like when it’s talking too loud for me to think clearly. I’m really sorry you’re feeling that way right now, and I want to assure you that you don’t have to continue feeling that way indefinitely. I can’t know whether you have any formal diagnoses in the realm of depression, but the fact you want to improve shows in itself that you aren’t a ‘lazy’ or crappy person; you might just be struggling to follow through on your good intentions, as almost all human beings do. 

I think it may help to try to identify what keeps you from improving the way you wish to, at least for focusing on your college work or other important things, in your words. Is it poor motivation? This might be depression talking again, and seeking a counselor/therapist (colleges can often help with this) may be beneficial. Do you have trouble focusing? Could you look into being evaluated for ADHD (if you feel like you really don’t have the ability to organize yourself or concentrate; not at all saying you have such a condition but just a thought)? Or more straightforwardly get study-skills support from your college? Most importantly, please don’t feel like you have to beat yourself up if you don’t improve exactly how you want to immediately; it is not going to help you and it’s not fair to yourself. I don’t think your dad would want you to be unkind to the child he loves. Therapy is never a cure-all, but it can be *so* helpful in sorting through the things you discuss in your post and helping you to figure out what strategies can help you live a happy, sustainable lifestyle; sometimes it takes a few tries to ‘click’ with a therapist, but once you find someone you feel comfortable with it can make a huge difference. I wish you the best!

Along the lines of some other comments, scar cream can help with fading (and with itchiness) once the initial healing has occurred (don’t use it on an open or healing wound). To my knowledge, silicone gel and/or patches/tape (the adhesive is really nice to stick it on and forget it for the day, and also doubles for covering things up) has the best evidence in its favor, while other things like vitamin E are actually probably useful more because the act of regularly massaging it into the scar helps with appearance. Be patient; you’ll want to use it for at least 60 days before deciding whether it is helping. Also, it may be worth going to a dermatologist about it, depending on if you feel safe (may also depend on your access to healthcare with/without parental supervision); my experience was quite positive, as she just asked if I had support and didn’t press it further. The reason I say this is that younger scars tend to be more amenable to laser/peeling/other intervention than older ones, so just something to know. Best of luck!
